Effect of Earthquake  
*541. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of EARTH 
SCIENCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Northern India was rocked be earthquake 
recently; 
  (b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have identified earthquake prone areas in the 
country; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
8 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) whether the local administration of these areas has been advised about 
the type of construction to be carried out in these areas to withstand the effect of 
earthquakes; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) The following two significant earthquakes have been experienced 
in the northern parts of India in the recent past: 
(1) An earthquake of magnitude 7.6 occurred on 8th October, 2005 at 09 
Hours 21 Minutes IST with its epicenter at latitude  34.5 degree 
North and longitude 73.2 degree East in Pakistan. The earthquake had 
caused extensive damage to property and loss of life in Jammu and 
Kashmir. The earthquake was also widely felt in other northern parts 
of the country including Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, 
Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Rajasthan and Delhi. Th e main shock 
was followed by several aftershocks of lower intens ities with 
decreasing frequency. 
(2) An earthquake of magnitude 5.9 with its epicenter a t latitude 36.9 
degree North and 70.6 degree East longitude in Hindukush-Afghanistan 
region occurred at 09 Hours 05 Minutes IST on 3rd A pril, 2007. 
The earthquake was reported widely felt in northern  parts of 
India including Delhi. 
 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) Bureau of Indian Standards [IS-1893 (Part-I): 2002], based on various 
scientific inputs from a number of agencies, has grouped the country into four 
seismic zones viz. Zone-ll, III, IV and V as shown in Statement-I (See below). Of 
these, Zone V is the most seismically active region, while zone II is the least. The 
Modified Mercalli (MM) intensity, which measures the impact of the earthquakes 
on the surface of the earth Statement-ll (See below ), broadly associated with 
various zones is as follows:

Broadlly, Zone-V comprises of the entire northeaste rn India, parts of 
Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttaranchal, R ann of Kutch in 
Gujarat, parts of North Bihar and Andaman & Nicobar islands. Zone-IV covers 
remaining parts of Jammu & Kashmir and Himachal Pra desh, Union 
Territory of Delhi, Sikkim, northern parts of Uttar  Pradesh, Bihar and West 
Bengal, parts of Gujarat and small portions of Maha rashtra near the west 
coast and Rajasthan. Zone-Ill comprises of Kerala, Goa, Lakshadweep islands, 
remaining parts of Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal, parts of Punjab, 
Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar Jharkhand, Chhatti sgarh, Maharashtra, 
Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. Zone-ll covers remaining 
parts of the country. 
(e) and (f) The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) ha s brought out 
several publications useful for construction practi ces in the country, which 
are required to be adopted for construction in eart hquake prone areas. In 
addition, National Building Code of India (2005), has also been brought out by 
BIS, which incorporates latest provision of relevant codes related to design and 
construction of earthquake resistant buildings. The  above-referred standards 
cover different types of construction and cater to the requirements of various 
parts of the country. Ministry of Housing and Urban  Poverty Alleviation has 
been advising State Governments for adopting disast er resistant construction 
technologies in the housing projects. 
To ensure construction of earthquake resistant hous es by strengthening 
techno-legal regime of respective States and UTs, a Model Town and Country 
Planning Legislation, Zoning Regulation Development Control and Building 
Regulation/Bye-laws for Safety against Natural Haza rds have been prepared 
by an Expert Committee constituted by the Ministry of Home Affairs. To help 
State Governments in amending their Acts/Bye-laws/R egulation, Building 
Materials and Technology Promotion council (BMTPC) has been organizing 
one-day Technical Workshops on Model Amendments in Town and Country 
Planning Act, zoning Regulation, Development and Co ntrol Regulation and 
Building Regulation for safety against natural haza rds in States/UTs to 
disseminate the recommendations of the Committee. T echnical Workshops 
have been organized in all 8 North-eastern States. In addition, Technical 
Workshops have also been organized in Tamil Nadu, C hhattisgarh, Bihar, 
Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Pondicherry and Andaman and Nicobar.

Private participation in Power Sector  
*542. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite repeated attempts  by Government to 
enthuse the private sector, it accounts for just 11 per cent of the country's total 
power generation capacity of 1,28,182 MW; 
(b) whether it is a fact that as the sale of electricity is not governed by the 
laws of the market, and the distribution sector is still reeling under losses, the 
private players are reluctant to invest money; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to prom ote the private 
participation in power sector? 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
Out of the total installed capacity of 1,32,329 MW as on 31st March, 2007, 
the installed capacity in the private sector was 17 ,112 MW which is 12.9 per 
cent of the total installed capacity. 
(b) The decade of the 1990s saw the gradual deterioration of the financial health of 
State Electricity Boards (SEBs). As a result, the Independent Power Producers (IPPs) 
which were required as per the then existing laws to sell their power solely to the 
host State Electricity Board, found it increasingly difficult to get financial closure 
in view of poor payment security. 
The Government of India has notified the Electricit y Act, 2003 which 
creates a liberal framework for the development of the power sector through a 
variety of initiatives like unbundling of vertically integrated power utilities, de-
licensing generation, allowing open access in transmission, recognizing power 
trading as a distinct licensed activity, setting up  of Regulatory Commissions 
and requiring the commissions to fix tariffs in a m anner so as to ensure 
financial viability of power utilities, etc. 
In order to ensure that the tariff for sale of elec tricity is determined 
competitively, the Tariff Policy was notified by th e Central Government in 
January, 2006, which provides that "all future requirement of power should be 
procured competitively by distribution licensees ex cept in cases of expansion 
of existing projects or where there is a State cont rolled/owned company as an 
identified developer and where regulators will need  to resort to tariff 
determination based on norms provided that expansion of generating capacity 
by private developers for this purpose would be restricted to one time addition of 
not more than 50% of the existing capacity. Even for the Public Sector projects, 
tariff of all new generation and transmission proje cts should be decided on 
the basis of competitive bidding after a period of five years or when the 
Regulatory Commission is satisfied that the situation is ripe to introduce such 
competition". 
Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides th at "the Appropriate 
Commission shall adopt the tariff if such tariff ha s been determined through 
transparent process of bidding in accordance with the guidelines issued by the 
Central Government". 
The restoration of the financial health of the State Electricity Boards/ State 
Utilities was recognized as the most critical challenge facing the sector. 
14 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
In this context, the distribution sector needed urgent attention to reverse the trend of 
deteriorating financial health of the sector. The reversal was sought to be addressed 
through a combination of the following key measures:— 
(i) control of theft of electricity. 
(ii) Reduction in the cost of supply through reduct ion in technical 
losses. 
(iii) Better management and lowering the cost of generation. 
(iv) Payment of user charge and Tariff rationalization. 
Further, the Government of India launched the Accel erated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) in 2002-0 3 aimed at 
effecting reduction in distribution losses under wh ich additional central 
assistance is being provided to the States for taki ng up various measures for 
reducing distribution losses. There have been improvements in billing, collection 
efficiency and the national average Aggregate Techn ical & Commercial 
(AT&C) losses of the distribution companies which h ave reduced from 
36.63% in 2002-03 to 34.54% in 2005-06. 
Encouraged by the Electricity Act, 2003 and other m easures, the 
Financial Institutions have agreed to consider fina ncial security arrangements 
other than Government guarantees. They have indicated availability of sufficient 
funds for good projects with viable tariff sponsored by credible promoters. 
(c) In addition to the above sector level initiatives, the Government have 
taken the following steps to promote private participation in power sector:— 
(i) One hundred per cent (100%) Foreign Direct Investment has been 
permitted on the automatic approval route in respec t of projects 
relating to electricity generation, transmission an d distribution 
(other than nuclear power plants). Recently, power trading has also 
been included in the above, subject to compliance w ith the 
regulations under the Electricity Act, 2003. 
(ii) Recognizing that cheaper power can be secured by reaping the 
benefits of economies of scale through development of large size 
power projects, the Government has taken an 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
initiative for facilitating the development of a fe w Ultra Mega 
Power Projects of about 4000 MW capacity each under  the tariff 
based competitive bidding route using cost effective super critical 
technology. 
(iii) The Government of India has been assisting wherever required, to 
resolve issues coming in the way of implementation of IPPs, 
including setting up of an Inter-Institutional Grou p (IIG) 
comprising of senior representatives from the Finan cial 
Institutions and Ministry of Power to facilitate ea rly financial 
closure of power projects. 
Encouraged by the enabling legislative framework an d the above 
initiatives, 16 private sector power projects aggre gating to capacity of 7320 
MW have achieved financial closure over last two years and have commenced 
construction.

†*543. SHRI AJAY MAROO: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the number of States where Electricity Boards h ave been 
constituted separately for generation, transmission  and distribution of 
electricity under the Electricity Act, 2003; 
(b) which States have not constituted separate Boards; 
(c) the reasons stated by the States for non-constituti on of the Boards; 
and 
(d) the action taken against the States which have not constituted their 
Boards?  
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRl SUSHIL  KUMAR  SHINDE): (a) 
to (c) Prior to the enactment of the Electricity Ac t, 2003, some States had 
enacted State Electricity Reform Acts, providing fo r reforms in their power 
sector. The Electricity Act, 2003 also has provisio ns for reorganization of the 
State Electricity Boards (SEBs). 
The State Governments of Assam, Maharashtra and Wes t Bengal have 
reorganized their SEBs under the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hi ndi.

The States of Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Karn ataka, Uttar 
Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan, Delhi, Gujarat and  Madhya Pradesh have 
reorganized their SEBs under their respective State  Electricity Reforms Acts. 
The Electricity Act, 2003 has saved those provisions of these State Acts which 
are not inconsistent with the Electricity Act, 2003. 
Section 172 (a) of the Electricity Act, 2003 provid es that the State 
Government may, by notification, authorize the SEB to continue to function as the 
State Transmission Utility (STU) or a licensee for such further period beyond the 
period of one year from 10.6.2003 (i.e. the date of the Electricity Act, 2003 coming 
into force) as may be mutually decided by the Central Government and the State 
Government. The State Governments of Bihar, Jharkha nd, Kerala, Punjab, 
Chhattisgarh, Tamil Nadu, Meghalaya and Himahcal Pradesh have, from time to 
time, authorised their SEBs to continue as the STU and a licensee under this 
provision of the Act. The Government of Assam has authorised the Assam SEB 
to continue only as a trading licensee. The reasons stated by these States in their 
requests to the Central Government for continuation of their SEBs as the STU 
and/or a licensee and the period of such continuation as decided by the Central 
Government and the State Government are given in the Statement (See below). 
Other States/Union Territories have Electricity Dep artments, except 
Tripura which has corporatized its Electricity Department.

Forecast by Indian Meteorological Department  
 †*550. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
Will the Minister of EARTH SCIENCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Indian Meteorolog ical Department has 
forecast that there will be 5 per cent less rain th an the average rain during 
the ensuing monsoon; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that several i nternational 
meteorological departments have forecast a good mon soon contrary to 
the said forecast by Indian Meteorological Department; 
(c) if so, whether any final forecast has been made to get rid of said 
confusion; and 
(d) if not the reasons therefor? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPlL SIBAL): (a) 
Yes, Sir. India Meteorological Department, based on the new statistical model 
predicted that the 2007 southwest seasonal (June to September) rainfall over the 
country is likely to be 5 per cent less than the long period average (LPA) (LPA:89 
cm based on 1941-1990.data). This forecast was made based on the data up to 
March, 2007. 
(b) Yes, Sir. It is true that several international meteorological institutes in US, 
UK and Europe have predicted above-average monsoon over India for the 2007 
southwest monsoon season. 
(c) and (d) These institutes prepare forecasts based on  coupled ocean-
atmosphere dynamical models, using initial data of April. They also take into 
account the EL-nino La Nina conditions. The dynamical models have reached the 
accuracy level of prediction of 7 days and research  work is going on to 
increase it to 10 days in nothern latitudes. Howeve r, the dynamical models do 
not give accurate forecasts in long term. However, some scientists in these 
institutes are trying to see whether the dynamical model will give reasonable 
accuracy due to averaging effects. This will take m any years to prove or 
disprove. 
IMD forecast is based on statistical method. A new method has been 
developed this year which gives in improved accuracy. IMD has more confidence in its 
synoptic and statistical methods for long range forecast than forecasts from these 
institutes that have stared these forecasts only recently. 
IMD will be issuing an updated forecast in June based on observation data up 
to May, 2007. More information on the evolution of sea surface temperature 
(SST) conditions (La Nina conditions) over the Pacific Ocean will be known by 
them.

National Curriculum Framework (NCF)-2005, seeks gui dance from the 
constitutional vision of India as a secular, egalit arian and pluralistic society, 
founded on the values of social justice and equalit y. NCF recommends for 
inculcation among children a respect for all people regardless of their beliefs. It

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
by 2010. The SSA promotes diverse strategies, speci ally targeting scheduled 
caste children. The SSA seeks to a develop context specific intervention to 
tackle the problems of education of scheduled caste  children. Some of the 
interventions of SSA are as follows: 
• Providing adequate infrastructure for elementary sc hooling in 
districts with concentration of scheduled caste population. 
• Freetext books to scheduled caste children from cla sses I—
VIII. 
• Provision of Rs. 15 lakhs to each districts for spe cial innovative 
activities to promote education of scheduled caste children. 
Two programmes for education of girls at elementary  level—the 
National Programme for Education of Girls at Elementary Level (NPEGEL) and 
Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV) have also been launched. Under the 
NPEGEL programme, special focus is given to educati on of girls from 
scheduled caste community. Kastruba Gandhi Balika V idyalaya scheme is 
specially targeted to provide schools with residential facilities at the elementary 
level for girls belonging to SC/ST/OBC and minority  communities. Out of 
2180 KGBVs sanctioned so far, 242 have been sanctio ned in scheduled caste 
dominant blocks. 16750 scheduled caste girls have b een enrolled in 1039 
KGBVs, operational so far, which is 27% of the total enrolment. 
NCERT operates the National Talent Search Scheme for pursuing courses 
in science and social science up to doctoral level and in professional courses like 
medicine and engineering up to second degree level subject to fulfilment of the 
conditions. Out of 1000 scholarships, 150 are reserved for scheduled castes. The 
National Institute of Open Schooling gives the SCI ST students concession in 
admission fees to the extent of Rs. 200/- for bridg e courses, Rs. 250/- for 
secondary courses and Rs.300/- for senior secondary courses. 
The National Literacy Mission aims to impart functi onal literacy to 
adult illiterates in the 15-35 age group. The main programme under the NLM 
include Total Literacy Campaign to impart basic lit eracy to the non-literates 
followed by Post Literacy Programme for reinforcement of literacy skills to the 
neo-literates and thereafter Continuing Education Programme

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
for providing opportunities for life-long educational opportunities. So far, the

scheduled tribes, females, minorities and other dis advantaged groups of people. 
It is estimated that 23% of the beneficiaries of literacy programme belong to 
scheduled castes.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) to (d) In pursuance of the judgement of the Supreme Court of October 6.1993 
in the Supreme Court Advocates on Record & Anrs. vs. the Union of India the 
judge strength of the High Courts is reviewed every three years. 
1. 1  As per the guidelines, the required strength of permanent Judges in 
a High Court is worked out by dividing the average institution of main cases 
during the last five years by the national average or the average rate of disposal 
of main cases per Judge per year in that High Court, whichever is higher. 
1.2 Similarly, the required strength of Additional Judges in a High Court 
is worked out by dividing the number of main cases pending over two years by 
the national average or the average rate of disposal of main cases per Judge per 
year in that High Court, whichever is higher 
1.3 If the disposal per Judge in the concerned High Court is below even 
the national average then instead of increasing the  strength, the concerned 
High Court is required to take steps for improvement in the rate of disposal of 
cases. If the average disposal of concerned High co urt is above the national 
average then increase in Judge strength is accordingly considered. The strength of 
Additional Judges is reviewed only if there is an i ncrease in the arrears of the 
pending cases during the last 5 years and the dispo sal per Judge is above the 
national average.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) 
Judicial Reforms is a continuous process and is a combined responsibility of all 
stakeholders including the Executive and the Judici ary. Both the Union 
Government and the State Governments continue their efforts including through providing 
financial support for carrying out and sustaining judicial reforms. The expenditure 
incurred by the High Courts including that for disposal of cases being charged on the 
Consolidated Fund of the State Governments, the States also have a major responsibility 
in this regard. In so far as the Union Government is concerned it is continuing its efforts 
for judicial reforms including that by providing fi nancial support to the State 
Governments by making budget provisions in this regard. Government approved a 
scheme for computerization of all District and subordinate courts of the country at 
a cost of Rs 442 crores. An amount of Rs.322.87 crore has been provided as Budger 
Estimates for 2007-08 for the Department of Justice for continuing both Plan and 
Non-Plan schemes aimed at efficient justice delivery. In addition to the Union 
Government's efforts, the States have also made appropriate provisions both for their 
respective High Courts and for its subordinate judiciary. 
(b) and (c) The 120th Law Commission in its Report of July, 1987 had 
mentioned that there was a justification for increasing the then ratio of 10.5 judges 
per million population to at least 50 million India n population. The Supreme 
Court, in its judgement of 21st March, 2002, in All  India Judges Association & 
Ors. Vs. Union of India & Ors. (all State Governments and Union Territories are 
also party to this case), directed that an increase in the Judge strength from the 
existing 10.5 or 13 per 10 lakh people to 50 judges per 10 lakh people would be 
effected and implemented within a period of five years in a phased manner to be 
determined and directed by the Union Ministry of Law. The Central Government 
have filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court praying that the increase in judge 
strength in the Union Territories for which Central Government is administratively 
responsible be allowed based on workload and pendency of cases. The matter is 
subjudice.

and (b) Under article 235 of the Constitution, administration of justice is a State 
subject and the State Government in consultation with its concerned High Court 
decides all matters concerning operations and setting up of courts. 
The matter of introduction of shift system in subordinate courts, among other 
things, was discussed in the Conference of Chief Mi nisters and Chief Justices 
of High Courts held in New Delhi on April 8, 2007. In that Conference all 
States had welcomed the introduction of shift system in subordinate courts and 
promised to work in that direction. It was decided in that Conference that 
evening/morning courts be set up, wherever found feasible, and appropriate cases 
including those involving petty offences be transfe rred to such courts. Either 
retired Judicial Officers be re-employed or serving  judicial Officers be given 
suitable incentive, to preside over these Courts. Government has requested the State 
Governments to take action on the above mentioned d ecision, as also on the 
other decisions of the Conference, in consultation with their respective High 
Courts. The Government has also requested that Chie f Justices of the High 
Courts to take action in consultation with the State Governments. 
(c) The Government has taken various steps/measures to improve the 
productivity and efficiency of the judiciary including periodically monitoring the 
pendency position in courts, grouping of cases involving common question of law, 
constitution of specialized benches, timely filling up the vacancies of judges, 
increasing the judge strength, organizing Lok Adala ts at regular intervals, 
encouraging alternative modes of disputes resolution like negotiation, mediation 
and arbitration and setting up of special tribunals  like Central Administrative 
Teibunals, State Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunals, Family 
Courts, Labour Courts, etc. The Government has also set up Fast Track Courts in 
States and has extended their term up to 31.03.2010 for clearing pending cases at 
District level. 
(d) and (e) The Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2006 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 23rd August, 2006, has among other things, a 
proposal to prevent the evil of witness turning hostile by amending sections 161,

Appointment of young judges  
4186. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any minimum age fixed for a person  to become a 
judge of any High Court; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what qualities does a person require to become a judge of a High Court; 
(d) whether it is a fact that some State Governments ha ve been 
recommending names of very young and untested people for appointments as 
judges in High Courts; and 
(e) whether Government will develop guidelines and conv entions to 
prevent nomination of very young people to High Courts? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) 
to (e) The minimum age limit for appointment of a person as Judge of a High Court 
from the Bar is 45 years. However, the Chief Justices' Conference held in December. 
1999 unanimously resolved that members of the Bar over 40 years and less than 
45 years may be recommended for appointment as Judges of High Courts only if 
they possess outstanding merit, and rigidity that t he members of the Bar must 
be above 45 years of age for being appointed must n ot be insisted upon. For 
the members from the Judicial service, they should not have crossed the age of 
58-1/2 years on the date of availability of the vacancy for the service quota. 
104 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
As per the Constitution of India, a person should have practised for at least 
10 years before becoming a Judge of the High Court. Besides this, his academic 
attainments, standing and experience, specialisations, if any, competence in 
perception, ability to deal with complex legal prob lems, grasping capacity, 
Judicial Patential like maturity, temperament, capacity to persuade and to be 
persuaded, patience, fairness etc., Integrity and character and antecedents are kept in 
view while considering a person from the Bar. 
After the Supreme Court Judgment of October 6,1993 in the Supreme Court 
Advocates-on-Record and Anr. Vs. Union of India, read with their Advisory 
Opinion of October 28, 1998, the entire process of initiation of proposal for 
appointment of a Judge of the High Court lies with the Chief Justice of that 
High Court. While making recommendations, the Chief  Justices keep the 
above criterion in view.

4268. SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Will the Minister of W OMEN 
AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether her Ministry is considering the demands of making the ICDS 
universal and regularize the services of Anganwadi workers; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and 
(b) In pursuance of the commitment of the Governmen t to universalize the 
Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme  as envisaged in the 
National Common Minimum Programme (NCMP), the ICDS Scheme has been 
expanded twice in the last two years. The first expansion was in the year 2005-06 
when 466 additional ICDS Projects and 1.88 lakh Ang anwadi Centres 
(AWCs) were sanctioned. Under the 2nd phase of expa nsion, during 2006-07, 
166 additional Projects and 106726 AWCs and 25943 Mini-AWCs have been

and Mini-AWCs has increased to 6284, 10.53 lakhs an d 36829 respectively.

The ICDS Scheme envisages AWWs and Helpers as "hono rary 
workers" from the local community who come forward to render the service on part 
time basis in the area of child care and development.

regularization of their services, does not arise.

523.    SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that out of one lakh deliverie s, 300 pregnant 
women die every year and with only an average of 16 point reduction in figure, 
India cannot reach its Millennium Development Goals of lowering the maternal 
deaths to 200 by 2007 and 109 by 2015; 
(b) whether this conclusion is based on the study repor t released by 
Government in October, 2006; 
(c) whether after receiving the report, strong Governme nt policies 
would be required to meet the target; and 
209 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
(d) if so, the steps Government propose to achieve the target set up by 
2015? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) Based on the official estimates of Registrar 
General of India (RGI), emerging from the Sample Registration System conducted 
between 2001-2003 the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) for India is 301 per 
1,00,000 live births MMR for India and major states is given in the Statement (See 
below). As per the report released in October, 2006, by the office of Registar 
General of India, titled "Maternal Mortality in India: 1997—2003 Trends, Causes 
and Risk Factors" the overall average rate of MMR decline during the period 1997-
2003 has been 16 points per year. At this rate of decline, as per the projection given 
by RGI it is expected that MMR would be in the range of 195—230 per 1,00,000 
live births by the year 2012. 
The National Population Policy 2000 and National Health Policy 2002 have 
set the goal of reducing MMR to less than 100 per 100,000 live births by the year 
2010. The Government of India is already implementi ng programmes to 
achieve the goals of reduction in Maternal Mortality Ratio. Accordingly, schemes 
and programmes have been developed to provide basic  health facilities 
especially in rural areas including those at the time of delivery. 
Government of India has launched the National Rural  Health Mission 
(NRHM) in the year 2005, with special emphasis on improving the health status 
of rural population throughout the country. Under the NRHM (2005-2012) and 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme Phase-ll (R CH-II) with the above 
goal in view, the GOI is strengthening services by implementation of the 
following key interventions: 
• Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), a scheme to promote Institutional 
Delivery for reducing Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR ) and Infant 
Mortality Rate (IMR) by providing quality maternal care during 
pregnancy, delivery and immediate post-delivery per iod with 
appropriate referral transport system along with ca sh assistance to 
pregnant women with a special focus on Below Poverty Line (BPL) 
women. The scheme also covers SC/ST women delivering in the Govt. 
Health Institutions and accredited Private Institutions.

Study on impact of global warming  
*528 SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that towns and cities along India's eastern 
coast would be devastated with global warming intensifying cyclones and rising sea 
levels eroding vast stretches of the shorelines; 
(b) if so, whether Government have done any comprehensive study on the 
impact of global warming in the coastal areas; 
(c) if so, the details there of; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefore? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (d) The Government is 
aware of the implication of the sea level rise due to projected climate change. 
The past observations on the mean sea level along t he Indian coast show a 
long-term rising trend of about 1.0 mm/year. The recent data suggests a rising trend 
of 2.5 mm/year in the sea-level along Indian coastline. Model simulation studies, 
indicate that the oceanic region adjoining the Indi an subcontinent is likely to 
warm at its surface by about 1.5-2.0 degree Centigrade by the middle of this 
century and by about 2.3-3.5 degree Centigrade by t he end of the century. The 
corresponding thermal expansion, related sea-level rise is expected to be between 
15 cm and 38 cm by the middle of this century and between 46 cm and 59 cm 
by the end of the century. According to a study con ducted by the Ministry of 
Environment & Forests on the impacts of climate cha nge on various sectors 
including coastal zones, in the event of one meter sea-level rise, 5764 Km2 of 
land in coastal areas of India is projected to lose , displacing approximately 7.1 
million people along with 4200 Kms of roads by the end of the 21st century. Further 
the coastal areas are also vulnerable to projected increase in 
218 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
frequency and intensity of extreme weather events l ike storm surges and 
cyclones. In the eastern coast, the vulnerable dist ricts include Jagatsinghpur 
and Kendrapara in Orissa and Nellore in Andhra Pradesh and Nagapattinam in 
Tamil Nadu.

*531.   DR.ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the observations ma de by 
Pakistan's Minister for Environment, on the sidelin es of Delhi Sustainable 
Development Summit, 2007 held during 4th week of January, 2007, that "India 
should focus on the environmental aspects of Siache n Glaciers which are 
melting at a faster rate due to global warming and continuous hu man traffic 
owing to heavy development of troops; 
(b) if so, what is the reaction of Government keeping the security of the 
nation in view.towards the suggestion of Pakistan's Minister; and 
(c) whether a comparative study has been made of other similar glaciers 
regarding the magnitude of melting rate where there is no human traffic? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) Y es, Sir. 
However, as per the information made available by t he Geological Survey of 
India, the total retreat of Siachen Glacier during the last 95 years (1909-2004) is 
about 500 meters at an average annual rate of 5.3 meter per year only. Thus the 
observations made by the Pakistani Minister are not  based on the factual 
data.Moreover, no proposal has been received by the 
224 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Government of India from Government of Pakistan regarding environmental aspects 
of Siachen Glaciers, although media reports from Pa kistan occasionally refer 
to the environmental benefits of the demilitarisati on of the area. Also, in 
proportion to the vastness of the Siachen Glacier, the actual deployment of the 
troops is small, which can have negligible effect on its melting.

of several Himalayan glaciers, including Siachen Glacier. These studies revealed

(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) Cholera, viral hepatitis, enteric fever and 
acute diarrhoeal diseases are the main water borne diseases caused by 
contamination of water with virus and bacteria, whe reas diseases caused by 
mosquitoes which mainly breed in water are vector b orne diseases like 
dengue, malaria, filariasis, viral encephalitis etc. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
World Health Organization, while assessing the association between climate 
change and health has projected that under warmer c limate conditions, 
stagnant water and scarcity of water will increase chances of cholera outbreaks. 
Changes in temperature and moisture would also incr ease the morbidity and 
mortality of vector borne diseases like malaria, Ja panese encephalitis and 
dengue. 
Health is primarily a State subject and provision of medical relief for water 
borne and vector borne diseases through primary and community health centres 
is looked after by the State Governments. The preventive measures taken by the 
local health authorities include provision of safe drinking water, improvement 
of personal and community hygiene, safe disposal of  human excreta, 
undertaking appropriate health education, surveilla nce and monitoring, 
distribution of chlorine tablets and ORS packets etc. 
A comprehensive National Vector Borne Disease Contr ol Programme 
(NVBDCP) is implemented through the States for prevention and control of vector 
borne diseases caused by mosquitoes. The strategies for control of vector borne 
diseases include disease management through early c ase detection and 
treatment, epidemic preparedness and rapid response . Integrated vetor 
management includes residual spraying, use of insecticide treated bed nets and anti 
larval measures. 
The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State 
Governments/Union Territories by providing funds under the Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme, Accelerated Urban Water Sup ply Programme, 
Total Sanitation Campaign, School Sanitation and Hygiene Education and Low 
Cost Sanitation Scheme for tackling quality related  problems in respect of 
rural and urban drinking water supply. National Ins titute of Communicable 
Diseases, Delhi (NICD) provides technical support t o the State Governments 
and undertake surveillance, early detection and pre vention and control of 
outbreaks of communicable diseases. 
An integrated approach has been initiated with Department of Drinking Water 
Supply to provide the technical support to monitor the quality of drinking 
water in different States so as to prevent occurrence of water borne diseases. 
232 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
The Government of India has also launched an Integr ated disease 
Surveillance Programme in November, 2004, to furthe r strengthen 
identification of outbreaks of various diseases including water borne and vector 
borne diseases so that early intervention could be made and occurrence, 
disability and death due to such diseases could be reduced.

(f) the obstacles being faced by entrepreneurs in sustaining Tuna fishing; 
and 
(g) the steps proposed to be taken by Government to  solve their 
problems? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) Governemnt has taken follow ing steps to 
encourage Indian entrepreneurs to operate Deep Sea Fishing vessels for Tuna 
fishing in Indian EEZ 
(i) an Inter-Ministerial Empowered Committee has be en set up to 
develop Deep Sea Fishing including tuna fishing. 
(ii) Indian entrepreneurs are being issued with Letters of Permission for 
Tuna fishing in the Indian EEZ. 
(iii) Overseas crew/technicians trained in tuna fishing are permitted to be 
engaged in the vessels. 
(iv) Government organizaitons have been equipped fo r conducting tuna 
resource assessment and development of trained manpower by acquiring 
modern Tuna fishing vessels. 
(v) Entrepreneurs are encouraged to diversify exist ing small and 
medium trawlers for Tuna fishing. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. Under the Centrally Sponsored  Scheme on 
Development of Marine Fisheries, financial assistan ce is provided to 
entrepreneurs for conversion of existing trawlers for resource specific fishing. 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
The subsidy is 50% of the cost of conversion with a  ceiling of Rs. 15 lakh per 
vessels. A scheme has been launched by Marine Product Development Authority 
also for diversifying small trawlers into monofilament long lining. 
(d) and (e)Alarge number of tuna long liners and tu na purse-siners 
belonging to serveral distant water fishing nations  are fishing in Indian ocean 
for tuna. However, no foreign flag tuna-fishing vessel is permitted to fish within 
our Exclusive Economic Zone. Indian entrepreneurs have been slow in extending 
their operation into international waters for harve sting tuna, despite the 
technology and policy framework having been put in place by the 
Government. 
(f) and (g) Institutional finance, trained manpower  and shore-based 
infrastructure are the main obstacles coming in the way of developing tuna fishing. 
The Government is permitting drawal of duty free fuel, subsidy for conversion 
and permission for mid-sea-transshipment of catches to save the entrepreneurs 
from waiting in the ports. Other operational difficulties as and when brought up 
by the Industry are addressed by the Inter Minister ial Empowered 
Committee.

237

GHG emissions by agriculture sector  
3992. SHRI BHAGIRATHI MAJHI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the agriculture sector is the single largest sectoral source of 
Green House Gas (GHG) emissions in the country; and 
(b) if so, the efforts being made to lower such emissio ns without 
compromising the crop productivity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) No, Sir. As per the Ind ia's Initial National 
Communication to the United Nations Framework Conve ntion on Climate 
Change (2004), energy sector is the single largest (61%) contributor to the 
country's GHG emission budget. Agriculture contribu tes only 28% of the 
country's GHG emission budget. 
(b) Keeping the future intensification of agriculture in view, the country 
has made several efforts in developing technologies  of mitigation, adaptation 
and risk reduction in agriculture. The technologies  involve balance fertilizer 
and water management, use of specific rice varietie s, and improved cultural 
practices.

SHRI NARESH GUJRAL:

4007. SHRI ABDUL WAHAB PEEVEE : 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that the country produces nearly eleven per cent of 
all the world's vegetables and fifteen per cent of all fruits, yet its share in global 
exports of vegetables is only 1.7 per cent and in f ruits, a meager 0.5 per cent 
only; 
(b) if so, what are the major factors which are undermining out country's 
potential for reaching super markets around the globe; and 
286 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the steps taken by Government to boost horticulture export? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) As per production database of the Food and 
Agriculture Organization (FAO) for the year 2005, I ndia's share in global 
production of vegetables and fruits was about 9.2% and 10.47% respectively 
and the share in global export of vegetables and fr uits was about 3.72% and 
0.36% respectively. 
(b) The major factors undermining India's potential for exports are :— 
1. Unorganized export sector. 
2. Lack of standards for farm & orchard maintenance in cluding 
presence of pest and disease. 
3 Lack of packaging standards. 
4. Lack of market information. 
5. Poor harvest infrastructure. 
6. Lack of proper cold chain and logistics facilities. 
7. Various non-tariff barriers imposed by importing co untries, 
particularly, the developed countries. 
8. Lack of awareness among farmers about producing goo d quality 
and safe produce. 
9. Lack of trained Horticulture manpower. 
10. High transport costs. 
(c) The steps taken by Government to boost horticulture exports are:— 
1. Training programmes for improvement in quality of p roduce and 
developed pre-harvest and post harvest protocols for export of grapes, 
mangoes, litchis, oranges, apples, kinnows etc. 
2. Export standards for 34 fruits and vegetables to EU  have been 
prepared and notified under the Agmark Act. 
3. Schemes for registration/recognition of Pack houses / processing 
units have been introduced for fresh fruits and veg etables 
particularly mangoes and grapes, meat, poultry, dairy, floriculture, 
peanuts, rice and cereal sectors.

Produce of India" is in operation for the processing/export. 
5. Promoting commercial research for benefit of proces sors/

various organizations under ICAR/CSIR system and Ag riculture 
Universities. Creation of awareness among the farme rs regarding 
orchard practices for qualitative production has been undertaken. 
6. Further the Department of Commerce through APEDA is  
implementing the concept of Agri Export Zones (AEZ) which aims 
at overall development of the supply and value chai n of the 
identified commodities in a contiguous geographical region, having 
export potential, in collaboration with the State a nd Central 
Government agencies.

through Commodity Boards, Export Promotion Councils  and 
Commodity Associations. In order to boost export of  agro 
products, the Government, provides various incentiv es for 
infrastructure development, quality control, market development and 
promotion, packaging, publicity, information dissem ination etc. 
besides providing assistance to exporters for condu cting publicity 
campaigns, market surveys, sending delegations abro ad, 
participating in international trade fairs, inviting potential buyers etc. 
Further, initiatives include awareness amongst farm ers about the 
latest techniques of farming through mass media sup port to 
agriculture through Doordarshan. In order to dissem inate 
information on improved production technologies amo ngst the 
farmers, block demonstrations and Integrated Pest Management (IPM) 
demonstrations are organized through State Department of Agriculture 
and Frontline Demonstrations through Indian Council of Agricultural 
Research. 
8. The Government has introduced a number of initiativ es and 
interventions for enhancement of production and pro ductivity of 
agricultural products, which inter-alia include Integrated 
Schemes under National Horticulture Mission for int egrated 
Development of Horticulture, and Micro-irrigation.

Use of chemical fertilizers  
4009. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether continuous use of chemical fertilizers has deleterious effects 
on soil fertility; 
(b) whether, to increase the foodgrains production, the  farmers are just 
injecting a lot of nitrogen and thus doing damage to our agriculture; 
(c) if so, the steps taken to educate the farmers about  judicious use of 
chemical fertilizers; and 
(d) whether organic food is having good nutrient value and if so, the 
measures taken to bring awareness among farmers to use organic source of 
nutrients to produce nutrientional food? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The  average 
consumption of chemical fertilizers in the country is 104.5 Kg./ha. (NPK 
nutrients) which is far less than other developing countries. There is no 
indication of large scale degradation of soil healt h and crop productivity in 
the country due to use of chemical fertilizers. How ever, there are few 
instances of deterioration of soil fertility/ certa in nutrient deficiencies in 
some parts of the country, especially in Indo-Gange tic plains due to 
inadequate and imbalanced use of chemical fertilizers. 
(c) The Government is promoting Integrated Nutrient Man agement 
(INM), which envisage soil test based balanced and judicious use of chemical 
fertilizers including secondary and micronutrients in conjuction with organic 
manures and bio-fertilizers under various schemes. 
(d) Organic Food is normally of good nutritional value.  The 
Government is promoting the production, promotion, certification and market 
development of organic produce in the country under various schemes.

308 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the percentage of those rural households who are 
not having enough food everyday in some months is highest in West Bengal, 10.6 per cent, 
followed by Orissa, 4.8 per cent and Assam 3.6 per cent; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to ensure that all people in the 
country get enough food daily ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION ( DR. AKHILESH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) No, Sir. On the basis of the results of National Sample Survey (NSS) 
61st Round (2004-05), survey data on household consumer expenditure Report No. 
512(61/1.0/5) conducted by National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), it is seen 
that, in rural as well as urban areas members of households getting enough food 
throughout the year has increased. Also, the number  of households in which 
members were not getting enough food has decreased. 
(b) In the Report conducted by National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), it has 
been estimated that the percentage of households not getting enough food every day in 
any month of the year is 1.3% in West Bengal, 1.3% in Orissa and 0,6% in Assam. 
(c) For ensuring food security particularly to the poor citizens, the Targeted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS) is being operated. The TPDS is primarily focused to cover the 
Below Poverty Line (BPL) families. The poorest of the poor among them are covered 
specifically under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY). Foodgrains are being distributed at 
highly subsidized prices to BPL and AAY poor families all over the country under the TPDS 
@ 35 kg per household per month. Foodgrains are also being distributed to States and Union 
Territories for different sections of societies under several welfare schemes. 
In addition to above the open market also takes care of the food needs of citizens. 
The Government keeps a continuous watch on the food situation and whenever there arise 
situations of shortage, the Government intervenes to import food items and makes them 
available in the market to augment supplies.

Central Government has made an additional allocation of wheat for the APL

report in October 2005. NCAER has inter alia recommended to restrict the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) According to the 
report of the High Powered Committee on Hazardous wastes constituted by the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court and the assessment of waste g eneration carried out in 
accordance with the Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) amendment 
Rules, 2000, about 4.4 million tonnes of hazardous wastes are generated annually in 
our country. The improper handling and indiscriminate disposal of such wastes are 
likely to cause environmental pollution. 
(c) The Government of India has notified the Hazard ous Wastes 
(Management and Handling) Rules, 1989 under the Env ironment (Protection) 
Act, 1986, which were amended in 2000 and 2003. The se rules regulate the 
generation, collection, storage, treatment, disposa l, export and import of 
hazardous wastes. According to these rules, all haz ardous wastes are required 
to be treated and disposed of in specially designed secured landfills. These rules as 
amendd in 2003 provide for the development of a com mon hazardous waste 
Treatment Storage and Disposal Facility (TSDF) thro ugh joint-venture 
partnership. The Ministry of Environment and Forests provides financial assistance 
in the form of Central Government subsidy to the tu ne of Rs. 2.00 crores for 
setting up of such facilities provided a matching g rant is given by the State 
Government. 
The amendments to these rules in 2003, provide for channelization of 
repyclable wastes listed in Schedule 4 of the rules. A procedure for 
326 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
registration of the recyclers has been laid down un der Rule 19 of the 
Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) amendmen t Rules, 2003. 
According to these rules, all hazardous wastes recyclers are required to obtain 
consents under Water (Prevention and Control of Pol lution) Act, 1974 and Air 
(Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and authorization under the Hazardous

Control Board is monitoring the ambient air quality  of Delhi at Nizamuddin,

Clearance of River Yamuna  
4047. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI : Will the Minister of 
ENVIORNMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that inspite of spending colos sal amount the 
condition of the River Yamuna have not yet improved; 
(b) if so, whether Government are having any action pla n against the 
agencies failed to clear the Yamuna; and 
(c) if so, what are those agencies and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (c) while the water 
quality of River Yamuna is within the prescribed li mits in the State of 
Haryana, it has not shown the desired improvement in Delhi and some parts of 
UP. because of phenomenal increase of population up stream of the river and 
large scale extraction of water from the river for drinking and other purposes. The 
National River conservation Directorate under the Ministry of Environment & 
Forests has launched Yamuna Action Plan (YAP)-I and  YAP-II at a total cost 
of Rs. 1339 crore for the abatement of pollution of  River Yamuna. An 
expenditure of Rs. 686 crore is reported to have been incurred under both the phases 
of YAP till 31 st  December, 2006. YAP-I was declared completed in Fe bruary, 
2003 and YAP-I with an estimated cost of Rs. 624 cr ore, is under 
implementation in the States of U.P., Haryana & Delhi with funds released from 
time to time commensurate with the progress of the sanctioned works in these 
States. Tackling of pollution in rivers is a contin uous activity and concerted 
efforts are undertaken on an ongoing basis by ail s takeholders viz; the Central 
Government, the States and the implementing agencies through various pollution 
abatement works like Interception and Diversion (l&D) works,' construction of 
Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs), Low Cost Sanitation  (LCS) works, 
Construction of Crematoria (CRE), River Front Development (RFD) works and 
other measures like plantation, public awareness etc. In addition to the above, the 
Governments of the NCT of Delhi, Haryana and U.P. h ave also taken up large 
scale sewerage, non-sewerage and sewage treatment works out of their own Plan 
funds. Besides continuous monitoring by the Ministr y, regular review of the 
implementation of the programme is undertaken by th e Ministry at different 
levels with the concerned State/ 
346 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
implementing agencies and the States are advised to expedite the progress of works 
based upon the review. 
Effect of global warming  
4048. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of 
ENVIORNMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that country would los e many 
hectares of land due to global warming by the end of this century; 
(b) if so, what stretegy has been formulated by Government to identify the 
affected areas; 
(c) whether Government have prepared any blue-print for  the 
rehabilitation of affected people and evacuate the likely and already affected areas; 
and 
(d) how much land has been lost by our country in the coastal areas due to 
global warming during this century and what is the rate of rise of sea level 
right now compared to last decades? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) The Government is aware of the implications due to projected climate 
change and the past observations on the mean sea level along the Indian coast 
show a long-term rising trend of about 1.0 mm/year.  The recent data suggests 
a rising trend of 2.5 mm/year in the sea-level alon g Indian coastline. Model 
simulation studies indicate that the oceanic region  adjoining the Indian 
subcontinent is likely to warm at its surface by about 1.5-2 degree Centigrade by 
the middle of this century and by about 2.3 -3.5 degree Centigrade by the end of 
the century The corresponding thermal expansion, related sea-level rise is expected 
to be between 15 cm and 38 cm by the middle of this century and between 46 
cm and 59 cm by the end of the century. According t o a study conducted by 
the Ministry of Environment & Forests on the impacts of climate change on various 
sectors including coastal zones, in the event of one meter sea-level rise, 5764 km 2 of 
land in coastal areas of India is projected to lose , displacing approximately 7.1 
million people along with 4200 km of roads. Further the coastal areas are also 
vulnerable to projected increase in frequency and 
347 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007) 
intensity of extreme weather events like storm surges and cyclones. In the eastern 
coast, the vulnerable districts include Jagatsinghpur and Kendrpara in Orissa and 
Nellore in Andhra Pradesh and Nagapattinam in Tamil Nadu. 
The Government appointed an "Expert Committee on Impacts of Climate 
Change with following Terms of Reference: 
(a) To study the impacts of anthropogenic climate change on India. 
(b) To identify the measures that we may have to lake in the future in relation to 
addressing vulnerability to anthropogenic climate change impacts 
(c) Any other matter relevant to (a) and (b) above.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND  
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Und er the 
National Family Welfare Programme, there is no inje ctable contraceptive

(i) Cyclofem—one monthly injectable contraceptive u nder phase-III

(iii) DMPA—Though this 3 monthly injectable is not included in the

Statement-I 
Details of success and adverse effects of NET-EN  
At the initiative of Department of Family Welfare ( GOI), the National 
Institute for Research in Reproductive Health (NIRRH), Mumbai had initiated a 
multicentre study on 2 monthly injectable contracep tive(Norethisterone 
Enanthate) after enrolling 1209 women across India. The approved duration of 
injection in the study was 4 years. The study has b een recently completed. 
The objectives were to assess user acceptability and 
350 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
continuation rates of this injection, to study side effects and also women's views 
and attitudes towards injectable contraceptives. The major emphasis of this study 
was on counseling by skilled councilors and quality services to the users. The 
results are very reassuring. The observations based  17268 months of injection 
use show cumulative continuation rates at the end o f 12,13 and 24 nonths as 
65%, 53.6% and 48.3% respectively. It was interesti ng to note that 39% of 
women requested to provide them injections beyond s tudy period of 2 years. 
Over 79% were satisfied with the method. About 89% said that the injectable 
should be available in our national programme and a lso 79% of them would 
recommend this method to their friends and relatives. The method was acceptable 
by the majority of women and was found very effecti vely, the cumulative 
method failure rate was 0.3% at the end of one year. 
There was no adverse effect no general or reproduct ive health 
necessitating hospitalization. About 91% of women c onceived within 12 
months and majority (52%) within 6 months after the  discontinuation of 
injection was over. 
The study is now nearing completion.  
Statement-ll 
Details of success and adverse effects of CYCLOFEM  
ICMR has conducted a study on monthly injectable co nraceptive, 
Cyclofem through its network of Human Reproduction research Centres 
(HHRCs). A total of 63,784 women attended family pl anning clinics at 15 
HHRCs of the Council were given a balanced presenta tion of all the 
contraceptive methods available in the national pro gramme including 
Cyclofem (Cafeteria a crpach). Out of these 26,856 (42.3%) accepted 
Tubectomy, 116 (0.2%) couples opted for the Vasecto my, 25% accepted 
condoms, 15.8% accepted IUD, 14.7% accepted Oral pi lls and monthly 
injectable cyclofem was opted by 1330 (2.1) of total family planning seekers. 
A total of 1330 women have been enrolled in the study and observed for 
11518 women months of use. Mean age of acceptors is 26.0+4.1 years and mean 
parity of 18+1.0 Mean weight and height of acceptors is recorded as 48.2+10.9 
kgsand 152.3+17.7 cms respectively. 87% of the acce ptors are literate and 
17.8% are employed. 
351 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May,2007 ] 
539 women have used 12 injections. The continuation rates at 6,9 and 12 
months are 79.2,73.9 and 70.3 per 100 users respect ively. Majority of the 
discontinuations were due to menstrual irregularities 9.2 per 100 users at one year, 
(discontinuations due to ammenorrhoea was 2.2,2.4 and 2.7 at 6,9, and 12 months, 
discontinuation due to heavy and prolonged bleeding were 1.9,2.1 and 2.7). Infrequent 
and reduced bleeding did not result in women discon tinuing the method. 
Discontinuations due to personnel reasons were 4.7,7.0 and 8.4 at 6.9 and 12 
months of use. 
No method failure has been reported in this study. Discontinuation rate due to 
other medical reasons like nausea, vomitings, High Blood Pressure, Rashes and 
itching, Weight gain and Breast tenderness were 2.2,3.5 and 3.8 at 6,9 and 12 
months. 
116 women discontinued from the study due to personal reasons like transfer to 
other city (56), husband separated (18) objection from family members (16) and illness of 
the husband (12) were the majore personal reasons for discontinuations. 
The study has just completed and the final reports have been received in the Health

from 2005. The policy envisages a key role for the Central Government in designing 
programmes with active participation of the State Governments and other stake 
holders in implementing these programmes. 
Of the targets set for the years 2005 and 2006, goa ls have already been 
achieved in respect of eradication of YAWS, Leprosy , establishing of an 
Integrated System of Surveillance and putting in pl ace a system of National 
Health Accounts in the Ministry while for eradication of polio revised target is end 
2008. In respect of other targets, planning efforts have already been initiated to 
achieve the time bound goals. 
(b) Health is primarily a state subject and it is for the State Governments to 
regulate the functioning of the private hospitals/c linics under their jurisdiction. 
A few states have enacted laws for regulation of private hospitals and clinics. At 
present there is no regulatory authority at the Cen tral Government level to 
regulate private hospitals.

FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

pneumonia in the world are in India;

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the reasons for not taking proper steps by Governme nt for 
protection of children who are the next generation of the nation; and 
(d) the steps being taken for safely and protection of children from this 
and similar other diseases?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND  
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) As per the 
State of the World's Children, 2006, brought out by UNICEF, India is the highest 
in the world in terms of absolute number of births and infant deaths. It is a fact that 
16 lakh infants die each year and out of which 11 lakh die during the first month 
of birth. The majority of deaths (19%) druing the first year of birth are due to 
pneumonia. 
(b) As per information available from the Central Burea u of Health 
Intelligence (CBHI), the number of cases and deaths due to pneumonia, gender-
wise and State/UT-wise for the last three years, as received in the monthly reports 
from Directorate of Health Services is given in the  Statement I, II and III. 
[See below) 
(c) and (d) Child Health has been a part of the Family Welfare Programme of the 
Government since 1977 and the measures taken have succeeded in reducing Infant 
Mortality Rate from 140/1000 live births in 1975 to 58/1000 live births in 2005. The 
steps currently being taken for safety and protection of children from this and similar 
other diseass are implementation of the Integrated Management of Neonatal and 
Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI) strategy, which adopts a holistic approach to the 
management of the commonest causes of neonatal and childhood moraltiy—
sepsis, acute respiratory infections (pneumonia), diarrhea, measles and malaria, all 
compounded by malnutrition. IMNCI will be implemented throughout the country in 
a phased manner. In addition, thrust is being given to ensure institutional deliveries and 
train health personnel on essential newborn care so that skilled attendance at birth 
is available and all newborns recieve specialized care. Efforts to deliver new born care, 
both facility based as well as home based, are bein g made. Micronutrient 
supplementation with Vitamin A, Iron Folic Acid and Zinc are being made. Infant 
and Young Child Nutrition are being stressed. Immunisation is one of the thrust areas 
of the ongoing Reproductive and Child Health Programme. The National Rural 
Health Mission, launched in April, 2005 for a period of 7 years (2005 to 2012) is an 
overarching intervention with a holistic approach and has envisaged reduction in Infant 
Mortality and Neonatal Mortality as one of the prime goals to be achieved.

  4062.    MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
  DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: 
SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in the country a woman di es at every 7 
minutes due to pregnancy related complications and more than 30 per cent 
cases go unreported; 
(b) whether country has one of the worst statistics as far as maternal 
mortality is concerned and even Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are better placed; 
and 
(c) if so, what is the action plan of Government to address this issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND  
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) Based 
on the official estiamtes of Registrar General of I ndia (RGI), the Maternal 
mortality Ratio (MMR) for India is 301 per 100,000 live births (SRS 2001-03 given 
in Statement. [Refer to the statement appended to t he Answer to Starred 
Question No. 523 (a) to (d)]. This translates into an absolute number of maternal 
deaths of aproximately 77,000 per year or in other words one woman dying 
every seven minutes due to complications related to  pregnancy and child birth. 
As per the same RGI survey report, "the precise number of maternal deaths is 
difficult to estimate due to overall limitation res ulting from the fact that 
maternal deaths are a small percentage of total dea ths in the country". 
Therefore it would also be difficult to estimate th e percentage of unreported 
cases. 
As per the World Health Report 2005,42 countries have MMR higher than 
India. Given in Statement (See below). As per the s ame report MMR of 
Bangladesh is 380 per 1,00,000 live births and that  of Sri Lanka is 92 per 
1,00,000 live births. 
Government of India has launched the National Rural  Health Mission 
(NRHM) in the year 2005, with special emphasis on improving the health status 
of rural population through out the country. Under the NRHM (2005-2012) and the 
RCH Programme Phase-ll (2005-2010) with the above goal

Cancer in North Eastern States  
4063. SHRI P.R. RAJAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have noticed a report that North-Eastern States 
have more number of cancer patients;   . 
(b) if so, whether Government would study the reasons f or this, if any; 
and 
(c) whether Government would provide more financial aid to these States 
to fight cancer? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND  
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Population 
Based Cancer Registry Programme (PBCR) of Indian Co uncil of Medical 
Research (ICMR) shows occurrence of certain types o f cancer e.g. 
Oesophagus, Lung, Mouth, Nasopharynx, Stomach, etc.  relatively higher in 
North Eastern Region as compared to other parts of the country. 
(b) The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has a lready 
initiated a multi centric study entitled "Role of T obacco use and pesticides 
exposure in causation of cancer" since tobacco is one of the main causes of cancer 
including oral cancer. 
(c) To provide efficient and cost effective treatment to cancer patients in 
North Eastern Region, this Ministry has recognized three Regional Cancer Centres 
namely Dr. B.B. Cancer Institute, Guwahati, Regiona l Institute of Medical 
Sciences, Imphal and Civil Hospital, Mizoram which are catering to the needs of 
the cancer patients. In addition to above, grant-in-aid has also been provided to 
Medical Colleges/Hospitals for purchase of equipment under other scheme of the 
National Cancer Control Programme. As a policy deci sion, 10% of the total 
budget of NCCP for the year 2007-08 has been earmarked for NE Region. 
Banning of medicines having toxic contents  
4064. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
410 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that some countries like Australia, US and UK have 
banned some of India traditional medicines due to presence of higher toxic metal 
content; 
(b) if so, what it Government's stance on this issue; 
(c) whether Government have made any regulatory/monitoring system to test 
the metallic content mandatory for traditional drugs meant for exports; 
(d) whether those medicines which are banned by these c ountries are 
presently in domestic use; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND  
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. After 
publication of an article in the Journal of America n Medical Association 
(JAMA), some regulatory agencies in other countries have issued health alerts 
regarding Ayurvedic India/ Unani medicines due to alleged presence of heavy 
metals above permissible limits. 
(b) and (c) The Government have taken following steps:— 
(i) Government has introduced mandatory testing for heavy metals in all 
purely herbal Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani medicines to be exported 
which is effective from 01.01.2006 onwards. This has been done to 
meet the regulatory requirements of importing countries. 
(ii) State Drug Licensing Authorities have been directed to ensure full 
compliance by all ASU drug manufactures of the provision of Rule 
161(1) and (2) relating to displaying on the lable of the container or 
in a leaflet to be inserted in the package of an AS U drugs, the 
true list of all the ingradients used in the manufa cture of the 
preparation together with the quantity of each of t he ingredients 
incorporated therein. 
(iii) Under Centrally Sponsored Scheme 29 State Dru g Testing 
Laboratories have been strengthened and 26 Private. Drug Testing 
Laboratories and other NABL accredited laboratories  have been 
approved for testing of ASU drugs in the country. 
411 

RAJYA SABHA [14May,20O?| 
(iv) A research project has been sanctioned to various laboratories of Council of 
Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) under the Goldern Triangle 
Partnership Project to study the physiochemical characteristics of 8 
most widely used Bhasmas and to carry out their toxicity studies. 
(v) Good Manufacturing Practices have been made mandatory for all Ayurveda, 
Siddha and Unani drug manufacturing units in the country. 
(d) and (e) The manufacturers of the medicines against whom Health Alerts have been 
issues by regulatory agencies of other countries have been asked to get their medicines 
tested for heavy metal and in case they are herbo-mettaic drugs to get their safety/toxicity 
tested, As per Ayurveda principles herbo-mettaic compounds following the detoxification 
process outlined in classicial texts are safe.

414

decline in the sex ratio is in the UT of Daman and Diu from 969 in 1991 to 710 in

(b) It is, nevertheless, recognized that mere legislation is not enough to deal 
with this problem that has roots in social behavior  and prejudices. Various 
activities have been undertaken to create awareness against the practice of pre-
natal determination of sex and female foeticide through Radio, Television, and

religious/spiritual leaders, as well as medical fraternity to curb this practice. The 
Government of India has also launched 'Save the Girl Child Campaign' with a 
view to lessen son preference by highlighting achievements of young girls.

polyandry, trafficking, rape, human trade. Examples have been observed in the 
vulnerably States, such as Haryana, Punjab wherein women are bought in from 
the economically backward States of the country, such as Orissa, Bihar, etc. by 
making payment. In the State of Haryana, polyandry has been seen to be 
practiced due to lack of women in the area. Such incidents may accelerate the 
cases of violence against women in the society.

Pesticides in fruits and vegetables  
  4080.    SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: 
SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the fruits and vegetables available in Delhi markets contain 
pesticides, bacteria and metals which are injurious to health; 
(b) if so, the steps taken to check the adulteratio n in fruits and 
vegetables; and 
(c) the arrangements made for making available good  quality fruits 
and vegetables? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND  
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) A 
Monitoring Study of Pesticide residues and heavy me tals in vegetables 
available in Delhi market has been carried out by t he all Indian Network 
Project on Pesticide Residues, Indian Agriculture R esearch Institute, New 
Delhi. 
A total of 54 samples of various vegetables (bhindi , palak, tomato, 
parwal, brinjal, cabbage) were collected from Agric ulture Produce Marketing 
Committee (APMC), Azadpur, New Delhi and analysed f or the possible 
residue of pesticides and heavy metals, during the period of June 2006 to 
April 2007. Out of the 54 samples, only in two samp les of palak and one 
sample each of cabbage and brinjal, residues of pes ticide cholrpyrifos were 
detected and the residues were below Maximum Residu e Limit (0.2 ppm). 
However, in rest of the 50 samples, no pesticide residues were detected. In the 
48 samples of aforesaid vegetables analysed for pre sence of heavy metals, no 
arsenic compound was detected and level of Lead and  Cadmium were found 
below permissible level. 
25 samples of various fruits and vegetables were lifted and analysed by the 
Govt, of N.C.T. of Delhi under the provisions of th e Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Act, 1954, during the period 2005 and 2006. None of the samples 
were found to be contaminated with fungus and bacteria.

Regulatory framework for SSIs 
4115. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Minister of SMA LL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to formulate a r egulatory 
framework for Small Scale Industries in view of fierce competitions; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
    (c) whether Government propose to implement the single window 
clearance system to establish Small Scale Industries; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) whether Government also propose to raise the financial limit of those 
units from Rs. 5 crore so that they may continue to  be covered under the 
Small Scale Industries? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) To facilitate the development of micro, small and 
medium enterprises (MSMEs), and to enhance their co mpetitiveness, the 
Government has enacted the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
Development (MSMED) Act, 2006, which has come into force with effect from 
2nd October, 2006. The MSMED Act, 2006 is facilitatory in nature, rather than 
being regulatory. The Act defines micro, small and medium enterprises, thus 
changing the concept from industry to enterprise.In  addition, the Act 
provides, inter alia, for a National Board for Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises as a statutory consultative mechanism a t the national level, 
notification of schemes/programmes for SMEs, prefer ence in Government 
procurements to products and services of the micro and small enterprises, 
more effective mechanisms for mitigating the proble ms of delayed payments 
to micro and small enterprises and simplification o f the process of closure of 
business by all three categories of enterprises. 
(c) and (d) The Government has already notified the  format of the 
Entrepreneurs Memorandum (EM) and the procedure of its filing under the 
powers vested in it by the MSMED Act, 2006. Although the grant of

clearances, including, inter-alia, the municipal clearances, the environmental 
clearances and other regulatory legislations, primarily vest  in the State Governments, yet 
the Central Government has been emphasizing the imp ortance of simplified 
methodology of clearance like the Single Window Clearance system for the establishment of 
micro, small and medium enterprises. 
(e) A new class of manufacturing medium enterprises with investment in 
plant and machinery between Rs, 5 crore and Rs. 10 crore has been notified as per
